passage: Ada, twenty-six, worked as a nurse in a hospice in Manchester. For the first year she went home shaken after every death. Her colleague Bilal, who'd been there a decade, told her he thought about his own death a little each morning, over tea. "It sounds grim," he said. "It's not. It reminds me what to do today." Ada tried it. She wrote down what she'd want said about her, and noticed none of it was about her job title. It was about calling her sister more, finishing the garden with her father, being kind on bad shifts. Over the months she felt calmer at work. She still cried sometimes. But she also phoned her sister every Sunday now.

qa.q: Where did Ada work as a nurse?
qa.a: She worked in a hospice in Manchester.

qa.q: How did Ada feel in her first year at the hospice?
qa.a: She felt shaken and upset after every death.

qa.q: What changed for Ada after trying Bilal's practice?
qa.a: She focused on relationships and small daily kindness, calling her sister and feeling calmer at work.

qa.q: How does Bilal see thinking about death?
qa.a: He sees it not as grim but as a reminder of what matters each day.

grounding: Shows a young nurse facing mortality calmly and reshaping her priorities around what will outlast her.

passage: The old-age home in Pune ran a Saturday storytelling hour, and Kiran, twenty-four, volunteered to record the residents' memories. One resident, Alka-ji, was ninety and sharp as a knife. She told Kiran about her husband, her classroom, the children she'd taught to read. Then she said, "When I go, these stories go too, unless you keep them." Kiran felt a chill, then a kind of steadiness. That night she couldn't sleep, thinking about her own life. What would she want remembered? Not her job, she realised. She began recording her own grandmother's stories on weekends. When Alka-ji died that winter, Kiran played her recording at the memorial. The room went very quiet. Kiran felt sad, but not afraid.

qa.q: How old was Alka-ji?
qa.a: Alka-ji was ninety.

qa.q: What did Kiran feel when Alka-ji spoke of her stories ending?
qa.a: She was shaken for a moment, feeling a chill, then felt steady and began thinking about what she would want remembered.

qa.q: What did Kiran do with this new understanding?
qa.a: She began recording her own grandmother's stories so they would be kept.

qa.q: How might Alka-ji's family have felt hearing her recording at the memorial?
qa.a: They likely felt moved and grateful that her voice and memories were preserved. 🤍

grounding: Shows a young volunteer reflecting on death and legacy and acting to preserve what matters.

passage:
Dear Noor,

Since Dadi died last month, I keep thinking about my own death. Not in a scary way, mostly. More like a question: what do I want to leave behind?

Dadi didn't leave money. She left recipes, the habit of feeding anyone who came to the door, and a lot of people who loved her. At her funeral, the neighbours talked about her more than about any of us.

I'm twenty-five, and I'm working sixty-hour weeks at a job I don't care about. I want to change that, slowly. I'm going to start teaching the evening English class at the monastery school again, and I'm writing down her recipes.

Some nights I still feel a flicker of dread. Then I think of her laughing in the kitchen.

Dolma

qa.q: What did Dadi leave behind instead of money?
qa.a: She left recipes, the habit of feeding anyone at the door and many people who loved her.

qa.q: What does Dolma mean by 'a flicker of dread'?
qa.a: Dolma still feels some fear about death, even while mostly thinking about it calmly.

qa.q: What steps is Dolma taking to shape a life that matters?
qa.a: Starting to teach the evening English class again and writing down Dadi's recipes.

qa.q: How might Noor respond to this letter?
qa.a: Noor might feel moved and encourage Dolma, perhaps sharing memories of Dadi too.

grounding: Shows a young adult reflecting on death after a loss and reshaping life around lasting values.

passage:
My grandmother's last notebook had grocery lists on one side and names on the other. People she wanted to phone. She got through most of them before she died.
For a while after the funeral I had this dread at night, like a clock ticking in my chest. Afreen, my friend from work, didn't try to fix it. She just asked, "So what would your list be, Zubin?"
That question calmed me more than anything. I started writing. It was short: my younger sister, two old teachers, the open-source library I maintain.
Now I document my code properly so someone else can carry it on. I call my sister every Sunday. I'm not fine with dying, I don't think anyone is. But thinking about it stopped feeling like falling and started feeling like sorting.

qa.q: What was on the two sides of the grandmother's last notebook?
qa.a: Grocery lists on one side and the names of people she wanted to phone on the other.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling at night after the funeral?
qa.a: Dread; Zubin describes it as a clock ticking in his chest.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's question help more than advice might have?
qa.a: It turned Zubin's fear into something to act on, so Zubin could choose what mattered instead of just sitting with the dread.

qa.q: How might Zubin's sister experience the Sunday calls?
qa.a: She likely feels closer to Zubin and valued, even if she doesn't know what prompted them 🤍

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from dread to calm about death by shaping his work and relationships around what will outlast him.

passage:
I share a flat with Aadhya in Bengaluru, so I notice things. After her uncle's funeral in March she was quieter for about a month. I'd hear her awake late, and once I found her on the balcony at 3 a.m., just watching the road.
Then something shifted, though I can't tell you exactly what. She left her ad-agency job for one at a school library, for less money. She started teaching the watchman's daughter to read on Saturday mornings. She wrote letters and sealed them in a shoebox labelled "later".
I asked her once if she was scared of dying. She thought for a bit and said, "Less than I was, Ira. More scared of wasting it." She said it lightly, then went back to covering library books.

qa.q: What label was on the shoebox of letters?
qa.a: It was labelled 'later'.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's answer, 'More scared of wasting it', suggest about her mindset?
qa.a: She seems to have made some peace with death and now feels more drawn to spend her time on things that last, like teaching and letters.

qa.q: How could Ira support Aadhya during the quiet month?
qa.a: Ira could stay close, offer company or tea on the balcony, and let Aadhya talk when she is ready without pushing.

qa.q: Why might Ira be unsure what changed in Aadhya?
qa.a: Ira only sees the outside, like the job switch and the reading lessons; she can't see Aadhya's private thoughts, so she can only guess.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's eyes, a young woman facing mortality more calmly and redirecting her work and time toward lasting things.

passage:
The Friday of the funeral. Afreen stood at the back of the crowded hall while person after person spoke about Urmila Ma'am, the professor who had supervised her master's. Nobody mentioned her publications. They talked about how she answered every student's email by midnight, and taught the watchman's daughter maths on Saturdays. Afreen went home and couldn't sleep. What would people say about her?
Two weeks later. The dread had turned into questions. She wrote in her notebook: What would I want to have done, if I had ten years? Twenty? The answers surprised her. Not the promotion. Teaching. Her sister's children. Her father's stories, recorded before they were lost.
Three months later. Afreen was tutoring two girls from her building on Sundays and recording her father's village stories every Friday evening. She still thought about death sometimes, but now with a calmer, almost practical feeling: then let me use the time.

qa.q: What did Urmila Ma'am teach the watchman's daughter?
qa.a: Maths, on Saturdays.

qa.q: How did Afreen's feelings change from the funeral to three months later?
qa.a: At first Afreen felt restless dread and couldn't sleep; later she felt calmer and practical, letting the thought of death guide how she used her time.

qa.q: What did Afreen's notebook questions help her do?
qa.a: Imagining ten or twenty years left showed what mattered, teaching, family and her father's stories, so she acted on them.

qa.q: How might Afreen's father feel being recorded every Friday?
qa.a: Her father would probably feel valued and touched that his village stories are being kept.

grounding: After a mentor's funeral, a young woman faces mortality and reshapes her time around what will outlast her.

passage: Sonali, you're asking why I still go to the library every morning at eighty. Let your Kalyani Paati tell you. When I was twenty-six, my dearest friend Revathi fell ill and died within a year. We were the same age. Before she went, she asked me to water the neem saplings she had planted outside the village school. I did it for months, crying into the bucket. And I kept thinking: if I went tomorrow, what would I leave? Some saris, some recipes. That frightened me more than death itself. So I started small. I collected twenty old books from neighbours and put them on a shelf in the temple verandah, with a notebook for borrowing. Then fifty books. Then a room. Revathi's neems are big trees now, shading the library door. I'm not afraid of dying, Sonali. I'm only afraid of wasting the mornings.

qa.q: What did Revathi ask Kalyani to water?
qa.a: The neem saplings outside the village school.

qa.q: What was young Kalyani feeling while watering the saplings?
qa.a: Kalyani felt deep grief, crying into the bucket, and a growing fear of leaving little behind.

qa.q: What was Kalyani's turning point, and how did it shape her legacy?
qa.a: Asking what she would leave if she died tomorrow; she started a small shelf of books that grew into the village library.

qa.q: How might Revathi have felt asking Kalyani to water the trees?
qa.a: Revathi was probably facing her death with care for what she had started, trusting her dearest friend to carry it on.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at twenty-six, her friend's death led her to build a library as her legacy.

passage: The visa appointment for Parveen's new job in Dubai was nine days away when her father's scan results came back. The doctors spoke gently: months, perhaps a year. That night, on the hospital's plastic chairs, Parveen felt a cold dread, and then an odd clarity. Anirban, her fiancé, brought tea and sat beside her. "A year from now, what will you wish you had done?" he asked. She knew at once. She would wish she had been here. She would also wish she hadn't thrown away the job Abbu was so proud of. They planned through the night. Parveen asked the company to defer her joining by six months; they agreed to four. She moved back into her old room. She recorded Abbu telling stories about his tailoring shop, and he taught her to stitch buttonholes, laughing at her crooked ones. When she finally flew out, Abbu, thinner, came to the airport and slipped his old scissors into her bag.

qa.q: How many days away was the visa appointment?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling on the hospital chairs that night?
qa.a: Parveen felt a cold dread, then an unexpected clarity about what mattered.

qa.q: How did Anirban's question help Parveen decide?
qa.a: Imagining her regrets a year ahead showed she wanted both to be with Abbu and to keep the job, which led to asking for a deferral.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel teaching Parveen buttonholes?
qa.a: Abbu would likely feel joy and pride, passing on his craft and sharing laughter in a hard time.

grounding: Facing her father's terminal illness and a job deadline, a young woman chooses time and legacy with him while keeping her future.

passage:
The cremation ground by the river was crowded with people from the office. Anand stood at the back, still in the shirt he'd worn to work. Professor Rao, who had taught him everything about bridges, had died in his sleep at sixty-one.

Afterwards, on the steps, his cousin Vijay sat beside him.

"You okay?"

"I keep thinking he had so many plans," Anand said. "A textbook. A lab in his village."

Vijay was quiet. "And what will people say about you, if it happened tomorrow?"

Anand felt a cold drop in his stomach. He thought about his last year: long hours, a promotion, weekend calls he'd skipped with his parents.

Over the next months, he changed small things. He called home every Sunday. He started teaching a free weekend class for engineering students who couldn't afford coaching, using Professor Rao's old notes.

On the first day, he wrote Rao's name at the top of the whiteboard.

qa.q: What had Professor Rao planned to create?
qa.a: He had planned a textbook and a lab in his village.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Vijay asked what people would say about him?
qa.a: Anand felt a cold drop of dread, as he realised how his last year had been spent mostly on work.

qa.q: What did Anand change so his life reflected what he valued?
qa.a: He called his parents every Sunday and started a free weekend class using Professor Rao's notes, investing in people and work that would outlast him.

qa.q: How might the students in the weekend class be affected?
qa.a: They get teaching they couldn't afford and inherit Professor Rao's knowledge through Anand, which may inspire them in turn.

grounding: A young engineer faces death after his mentor dies and reshapes his work and relationships around what will outlast him.

passage:
"Does it get easier?" Baljeet asked. "Being around dying people every day?"

Vasudha, a nurse at the hospice for two years, stirred her tea in the canteen. "Easier isn't the word. Calmer, maybe."

"How?"

"When I started, I was scared all the time. Scared of saying the wrong thing. Scared of my own parents getting old." She paused. "Then I noticed what patients talk about at the end."

"Which is?"

"Almost nobody talks about their job title. They talk about who they forgave, who they didn't call. One man asked me to phone his brother, whom he hadn't spoken to in twenty years."

Baljeet put his cup down. "And did the brother come?"

"He came. They didn't say much. They held hands."

"So what did you change?"

"I call my sister even when we've fought. I'm doing my master's in palliative care so I can teach younger nurses." She smiled. "I think about death more than you. But I'm less afraid of it."

qa.q: How long has Vasudha been a nurse at the hospice?
qa.a: Vasudha has been a nurse at the hospice for two years.

qa.q: How has Vasudha's feeling about death changed since she started?
qa.a: She was scared all the time at first, but now she feels calmer and less afraid, even though she thinks about death often.

qa.q: What did Vasudha change after listening to patients, and why?
qa.a: She calls her sister even after fights and is studying to teach younger nurses, because patients showed her that relationships and passing on care matter most.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see death differently after this conversation?
qa.a: Baljeet started curious and perhaps uneasy, but may now see thinking about death as a way to focus on relationships.

grounding: A young hospice nurse explains how facing death daily made her calmer and reshaped her relationships and work toward what will last.

passage:
Last March a truck skidded on the wet road and missed my scooter by maybe a metre. I sat on the kerb afterwards, shaking, and the thought that came wasn't dramatic. It was just: if that was it, what would be left?

I was twenty-five. My answer, honestly, was a pile of work emails and a good credit score.

For a few weeks I kept thinking about it, and it frightened me, then it slowly stopped frightening me and started organising me.

I wrote down what I wanted to outlast me. The small lending library I'd started at the bus stop near my old school, which I'd stopped stocking. My friendship with Aadhya, which I'd let drift. And work I'd be glad to put my name to.

So I restocked the library, and got two schoolgirls to run it with me. I called Aadhya and apologised for disappearing. I asked my manager to move me to the rural clinics project.

I'm Shalini. Death is still there. But it feels like a quiet guide now, not a threat.

qa.q: How far did the truck miss the scooter by?
qa.a: The truck missed the scooter by maybe a metre.

qa.q: How did Shalini's feeling about death change in the weeks after the near-miss?
qa.a: At first the thought frightened Shalini, but slowly it became calmer, like a quiet guide rather than a threat.

qa.q: What did Shalini do to shape life around what would last?
qa.a: Shalini restocked the library with two schoolgirls, reconnected with Aadhya, and asked to join the rural clinics project.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Shalini called to apologise?
qa.a: Aadhya might feel surprised and touched, perhaps relieved that a friendship that seemed to have faded still mattered to Shalini.

grounding: After a near-miss, a young adult reflects on mortality and reshapes relationships and work toward what will outlast them.

passage:
Hospice volunteer coordinator's note. Sarita.
Afreen, 24, has volunteered with us on weekends for six months. At first she was nervous around patients near the end of life. She'd talk too much, fill silences, avoid the word "death".
This month she sat with Mr Pinto, who had no family nearby. He asked her to read his old letters aloud. She did, for three Saturdays. He died on a Tuesday.
She came in the next weekend, quieter. She said she'd expected to feel terrified of dying herself. Instead she felt calm, and oddly clear about what matters. "He didn't talk about his job once. Only people."
She told me she's started calling her grandfather every Sunday and has asked to reduce her overtime at work.
I've made sure she has time with our counsellor too; grief for patients is real, even for volunteers.

qa.q: What did Mr Pinto ask Afreen to read aloud?
qa.a: His old letters.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel after Mr Pinto died?
qa.a: Afreen felt calm and clear about what matters, rather than terrified, though quieter than usual.

qa.q: What did Sarita do to support Afreen, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Sarita made sure Afreen had time with the counsellor, because volunteers grieve too and need support.

qa.q: How might Afreen's grandfather feel about the Sunday calls?
qa.a: Her grandfather would probably feel happy and valued, looking forward to hearing from her.

grounding: Illustrates a young volunteer facing mortality calmly and reshaping priorities around relationships.

passage:
Saturday night
Sarita here. Today was Kavitha's father's memorial. I went to support her and came back thinking about my own life.
Uncle was a post office clerk. Nobody mentioned his job. Instead, one person after another stood up: the neighbour's son he taught maths to for free, the widow whose pension papers he filled in every year, the boys from the cricket club he coached on Sundays.
Kavitha held my hand and said, "He always said, 'Do small things that stay.'"
On the bus home, I felt a flicker of dread, the kind I usually push away: one day people will stand up for me too. What would they say? That I answered emails fast?
So tonight I wrote down three things I want to outlast me: that I was kind to my parents, that I helped some younger people at work grow, and that I kept my friends. Tomorrow I'll call Kavitha. Then Amma.

qa.q: What was Kavitha's father's job?
qa.a: He was a post office clerk.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Sarita felt a flicker of dread about mortality, then grew calmer and clearer while writing down what matters.

qa.q: What did Sarita take from the memorial, and how could it shape daily life?
qa.a: Small, lasting acts of care matter more than a job title; Sarita can put time into parents, younger colleagues and friends now.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel when Sarita calls tomorrow?
qa.a: Kavitha would probably feel comforted and less alone in her grief.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult facing mortality after a memorial and reshaping priorities around what will outlast oneself.

passage: Three weeks after Aaja's cremation, Uday sat under the neem tree his grandfather had planted outside their house in the village near Nashik. The tree was older than Uday's father. People still stopped to rest under it on their way to the market. Uday had come home from Pune for the rites and stayed on, unable to shake a heavy, restless dread: one day this would be him, and what would be left? His cousin Pallavi sat down beside him with two cups of tea. "Aaja never talked about legacy," she said. "He just planted trees and taught every kid in the lane to read the newspaper." Uday laughed, and the dread eased a little. That evening he told Pallavi his plan: keep his job, but come back one weekend a month to run the reading circle Aaja had started. The next morning he watered the neem before catching his bus.

qa.q: Who planted the neem tree outside the house?
qa.a: Uday's grandfather, Aaja, planted it.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling in the weeks after the cremation?
qa.a: He felt a heavy, restless dread about his own death and what he would leave behind.

qa.q: What choice helped Uday turn his dread into purpose?
qa.a: Deciding to keep his job but come back monthly to run Aaja's reading circle, a practical way to carry on what mattered.

qa.q: How does Pallavi remember Aaja?
qa.a: Pallavi remembers him warmly as someone who never talked about legacy but simply planted trees and taught children to read.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing mortality after a grandparent's death and shaping life around what will last.
